transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-12-10
Time: 17:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Sara Kim (Redwood AE), Evan Park (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Acme CTO), Raj Patel (Lead ML Eng), Maya Singh (Platform Eng)

Summary:
Redwood ran an edge-cases demo focused on handling very long contexts (100k+ tokens), sustained high TPS (targeting 1.5-2k TPS), streaming responses under load, backpressure behavior, and timeout/fallback policies. Customer raised questions about determinism, caching, KV cache eviction, private deployment network constraints (VPC, egress), SOC2/SAML/KMS, and SLA for Dedicated. Redwood AE + SE proposed a 1-week POC including a Dedicated trial to validate p99 latency and streaming reliability. Several follow-ups and docs to be shared.

Topics Covered:
- API behavior for very long context windows and model chunking
- Console observability: per-route token breakdowns, streaming metrics, backpressure indicators
- Redwood Optimize recommendations: batching, quantization, autoscaling profiles
- Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs under 2k TPS
- Streaming backpressure handling and timeouts with fallbacks to shorter model variants
- Security: SOC2, SSO/SAML, KMS/HSM, audit logs and VPC peering

Transcript:
[00:00] Sara Kim: hi everyone thanks for joining, uh we went through the signup earlier, today Evan and I will run through some edge cases — long context, high TPS, and how streaming behaves when there's backpressure and timeouts.
[00:12] Lena Ortiz: yeah thanks, we mostly want to see real behavior — we have a payments flow that can attach massive audit trails to a prompt, so long contexts are real for us and we do sustained spikes at eod when batching clears.
[00:25] Evan Park: great, that's perfect context. quick overview: we'll demo the API calls, then the Console observability, and finally Optimize suggestions. we'll show a simulated 2k TPS load from a load generator hitting a Dedicated pool.
[00:37] Raj Patel: quick question — do you run the long context as single request or streaming chunked? we typically stream because responses can be multi-part.
[00:45] Evan Park: good call. we support both; for very long contexts we do prefix/KV caching and model chunking. for streaming we chunk tokens over a stream and we keep KV cache pinned in memory. when the context is > model window we fall back to external prefix store + recomposition.
[00:58] Maya Singh: what about determinism — if we hit a failover to a variant model during a spike, will outputs change significantly?
[01:06] Evan Park: there can be variance; our routing policy can be configured to prefer model variants that are architecture-compatible and quantization-matched to reduce semantics drift. we also do canary rollouts and shadowing to measure regressions.
[01:18] Sara Kim: we'll show the console traces that highlight model switch events and quality regs.
[01:23] [00:60] Evan Park: (demo starts) okay i'm firing the first scenario: 1) long context single-request of ~120k tokens using our chunking + prefix cache mode, model set to open-redwood-8k->we simulate extended window via chunking.
[01:42] Evan Park: transcript may be a bit rough here — but you can see p50/p90/p99 latency on the left, token breakdown middle, and streaming lag metric on the right.
[01:53] Lena Ortiz: p99 looks high 2.8s for a chunk? is that acceptable? our SLA target is under 1s for critical path.
[02:02] Evan Park: that's per-chunk — if you want end-to-end response for long-gen you'll see higher, but we optimize for tail by parallelizing per-chunk decode where possible and prioritizing lower-latency requests using a hot path. for the critical path you can configure a lighter model variant or enable our dedicated pool which gives predictable throughput.
[02:19] Raj Patel: can you show the batching configuration? our current router does simple 20ms batching but we had lots of timeouts when TPS hit 1.5k.
[02:29] Evan Park: yep — in Optimize we recommend adaptive batching based on sequence-length histograms. here's a recommendation: 1) minimum batch window 5 ms 2) max batch tokens 64k 3) dynamic scaling of worker processes. these are suggestions and we can auto-apply test profiles.
[02:45] Sara Kim: note that the Optimize suggestions also include quantization profiles — for high TPS we often suggest int8 on compatible models which reduces latency and memory footprint.
[02:56] Maya Singh: any risk to quality from int8? we care about answer correctness for regulatory copy.
[03:04] Evan Park: small drop in some cases, we surface regression traces and evals for your prompt sets. the console's quality monitoring ties regressions to specific commit ids and we can roll back.
[03:15] [03:20] Evan Park: next scenario: sustained high TPS — i'm spinning up a load generator to hit 1.8k TPS to simulate your peak.
[03:31] Evan Park: you'll see the Dedicated pool's autoscaler start additional replicas at about 1.2k TPS threshold per zone. we also have hot/warm worker tiers to absorb spikes.
[03:42] Lena Ortiz: what if autoscale lags and we start to see queueing — how does Redwood handle backpressure?
[03:50] Evan Park: two layers: 1) ingress rate limiting + priority queuing (critical requests get priority), 2) streaming backpressure signals — when workers are overloaded, they'll signal the router to slow down chunk emit and optionally return early partial responses. we also support fallback policies: automatic fallback to a lighter model variant or synchronous mode with a shorter timeout.
[04:10] Raj Patel: in practice do you drop streaming connections or do you buffer inside Redwood? we've seen buffers grow in our proxies and then timeouts cascade.
[04:19] Evan Park: we avoid unbounded buffering. the router maintains a bounded backpressure window and emits an RST-like event in the stream when the buffer limit is reached; clients should handle reconnect+resume semantics. for HTTP streaming we emit a structured partial response with status flags so your client can detect incomplete streams.
[04:36] Maya Singh: does the console surface these backpressure events?
[04:40] Evan Park: yes — streaming-lag and backpressure-rate are top-level metrics, plus per-client drop rates. you can set alerts for sustained backpressure > 5% over 10 minutes.
[04:50] [05:00] Evan Park: ok i'm toggling the scenario to force a model fallback mid-stream to show behavior.
[05:07] (chatter, keyboard clicks)
[05:12] Evan Park: you'll see the stream emit a partial chunk with code "fallback_started" and then the router switches to a faster quantized variant. there's a small discontinuity but we send a boundary token and annotate the transcript to help client reconciliation.
[05:25] Lena Ortiz: that's useful, but would prefer a stronger guarantee for critical flows — is there a way to pin a request to only one variant and fail rather than fallback?
[05:33] Sara Kim: yes, routing policy has a strict mode — pin_to_variant: true — which will refuse fallback and return 503 when capacity isn't available. tradeoff is availability for determinism.
[05:43] Raj Patel: about retries — if a streaming connection resets mid response, does Redwood support resume from KV cache or do we have to resend full context?
[05:52] Evan Park: for resumed streaming we support resume tokens when using the SDK. the server keeps KV cache for a short TTL (configurable) so a resumed connection within the TTL can pick up. outside the TTL, clients should resend prefix; Optimize helps minimize resend sizes by caching frequently used prefixes.
[06:08] Maya Singh: network constraints — we want Private deployment in our VPC with strict egress rules. can you confirm peering and no egress to public internet?
[06:16] Evan Park: Private (VPC) mode supports customer-managed networking; we can run in your VPC or on-prem. we use private peering and optional egress controls. KMS/HSM integrations supported for keys. we'll share the network diagram.
[06:27] Lena Ortiz: SOC2 and SSO details? we need SAML, RBAC and audit logs forwarded to our SIEM.
[06:35] Sara Kim: we have SOC2 attestation and support SAML SSO, RBAC roles, and audit log export (can forward to Splunk/Datadog). we'll attach the certs.
[06:44] [06:50] Evan Park: demo note: i'm switching to the Console's trace view to show a timeout scenario. here's a request that timed out at 15s and auto-fell back to a short-model which returned a partial structured answer.
[07:02] Raj Patel: I see the trace shows "timeout_policy: aggressive" — what are the policy options?
[07:07] Evan Park: you can set timeout_policy to conservative, aggressive, or strict. conservative will allow longer tail and queue re-tries, aggressive will fail fast and fallback to lighter models, strict will pin and fail if resource not available.
[07:18] Lena Ortiz: for compliance we may want strict for certain endpoints. is there an audit flag for strict mode usage?
[07:24] Evan Park: yes, every policy decision is logged with a decision_id and included in audit logs.
[07:29] [07:40] Sara Kim: ok next — Optimize. we ran an offline eval that suggests for your workload: int8 quantization on the inference model, prefix caching for the audit trails, and a dedicated pool with 3 zones to hit a stable 2k TPS. i'll share the spreadsheet.
[07:53] Maya Singh: how do you estimate cost saving with these changes?
[07:57] Sara Kim: Optimize projects token-level cost and CPU/GPU cost by scenario; for example switching to int8 saved ~28% GPU cost in a similar financial workload we tested. those are modeled in the spreadsheet.
[08:08] Raj Patel: any gotchas with streaming timeouts and SDK reconnection? we've had issues with idempotency in our gateway.
[08:15] Evan Park: best practice: attach a request_id and chunk sequence numbers; our resume token maps sequence numbers so you can dedupe. also consider stateless resumable receipts.
[08:26] Lena Ortiz: can you run a POC with our real payload distribution?
[08:29] Sara Kim: absolutely — next steps: we'll run a 1-week POC on Dedicated. we'll need sample payloads, expected TPS profile, and a list of critical endpoints. Evan will share the POC template.
[08:40] Maya Singh: timeline? we'd like results before Jan 5th.
[08:44] Sara Kim: we'll aim to provision by Dec 15th and run the week-long test by Dec 16-23, giving you a buffer to review results before Jan 5th.
[08:55] [09:00] (wrap up)
[09:03] Lena Ortiz: ok that's helpful. please send SOC2 + network diagram; also include dedicated capacity pricing and the Optimize eval spreadsheet.
[09:11] Sara Kim: noted — we'll send those. Evan, anything to add?
[09:15] Evan Park: I'll include sample load scripts and the resume token SDK snippet. also I'll add a checklist for client-side reconnection handling.
[09:24] Sara Kim: thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the docs and set a POC kickoff.
[09:28] Lena Ortiz: thanks all.

End of transcript.
